name: Relay

claims.claim_text: The stimulating coil in a home-built transcranial magnetic stimulation rig is an air coil with no magnetic core, formed simply by winding heavy-gauge wire.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's just some heavy wire wound up into a coil.
claims.speaker: Ben Krasnow
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Krasnow - Sprauncy Saccadic Spintherism

claims.claim_text: Magnetic stimulation works by using a relay to abruptly interrupt the coil current; the collapsing field induces current in nearby tissue, which is what produces the visible muscle twitch.
claims.quote_verbatim: Assumably with a relay and that then drops the field and then the – and then the current flows in your brain and then you show your hand twitching.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Krasnow - Sprauncy Saccadic Spintherism

claims.claim_text: Field strength from such a coil falls off with the square of distance, so the coil has to be held essentially against the target to be effective.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because it obviously drops with the square of the distance.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Krasnow - Sprauncy Saccadic Spintherism

claims.claim_text: Early computing was built from relay logic, and engineers pushed relay technology until they hit its intrinsic speed ceiling before moving to tubes.
claims.quote_verbatim: we worked with relay technology until we pressed it to the upper limits of its speed capability
claims.speaker: Howard Johnson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Howard Johnson - Winsome Waveform Wizardry

claims.claim_text: The speed limit of relay logic came from mechanical contact bounce: the moving levers ring rather than settling cleanly, which corrupts the switched signal.
claims.quote_verbatim: You know, in which case, you had trouble with ringing. You know, the little levers would actually bounce.
claims.speaker: Howard Johnson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Howard Johnson - Winsome Waveform Wizardry

claims.claim_text: Synchronously switching a large bank of relays coupled mechanically through the chassis: the whole machine vibrated hard enough to cause bit errors in unrelated parts of the system.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you did it synchronously and everything was going, the whole system would vibrate so much that it would cause bit errors in other places.
claims.speaker: Howard Johnson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Howard Johnson - Winsome Waveform Wizardry

claims.claim_text: Beyond speed, relay-based machines were limited by heat dissipation and by packaging problems, the same class of physical limits that later recurred with tubes, transistors and ICs.
claims.quote_verbatim: They had trouble with heat. They had all these problems with the packaging.
claims.speaker: Howard Johnson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr. Howard Johnson - Winsome Waveform Wizardry

claims.claim_text: A reed switch on its own is just a sealed glass tube containing two contacts; the coil that actuates it is a separate part, and only the coil-plus-switch assembly is a reed relay.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you're just talking about the read switch itself, there is no coil. It's just the glass tube with the two contacts.

claims.claim_text: Reed switches are a specialist product category with dedicated manufacturers such as Mida that build essentially nothing else, and the process involves a surprising number of high-precision steps.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're one of the big manufacturers, worldwide manufacturers of high-quality read switches.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: In industrial equipment the standby current budget is dominated not by the processor but by sensors, actuators and relays.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's not the processors that's sucking down on the current. It's all these, you're dealing with a bunch of sensors and actuators and relays.
claims.speaker: Tom LeMense
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom LeMense - Cacaesthestic Chronometric Carriwitchet

claims.claim_text: A latching or unenergised mechanical relay draws literally zero current in one of its states, which is why solid-state switches have not displaced relays despite vendors wanting to sell the replacement.
claims.quote_verbatim: But what's nice about a relay is in one state, it consumes no current at all
claims.speaker: Tom LeMense
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tom LeMense - Cacaesthestic Chronometric Carriwitchet

claims.claim_text: Packing relays tightly, as in a switching matrix, lets their coil magnetic fields couple into neighbouring relays and interfere with them.
claims.quote_verbatim: one trap with relays is that if you want to do matrix, you know, matrices of relays and you want to pack them close together, then they can actually interfere with each other. The magnetic fields can interfere.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The fix for dense relay arrays is to specify magnetically shielded relays rather than trying to space ordinary parts apart.
claims.quote_verbatim: You've got to get a magnetically shielded relay if you want to pack them tightly together.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Magnetically shielded ultra-miniature relays were developed for telephone switching exchanges, where thousands of lines had to be cross-connected in a small volume.
claims.quote_verbatim: they used to go in the phone switching exchanges and stuff like that. You know, you had to switch 10,000 lines
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: High-specification shielded relays of this class cost on the order of ten dollars each even in volume.
claims.quote_verbatim: And these relays cost like 10 bucks a pop in volume, some of them.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Off-state leakage adds in parallel across a matrix: an individual relay may offer about two gigaohms open impedance, but a thousand of them in parallel behave like a much lower resistance and degrade signal integrity.
claims.quote_verbatim: they each might have two gig ohms, like, you know, off impedance, right? Right. You know, leakage. But you put a thousand two gig ohm resistors in parallel
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A relay is fundamentally a mechanical device: a magnetic coil physically moves a strip of metal into contact with another piece of metal to make the connection.
claims.quote_verbatim: A relay is basically you have a strip of metal and you use a magnetic coil and you move... You physically move that coil or that piece of metal to contact another piece of metal and that creates a connection.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Because the contact armature is moved magnetically, a stray external magnetic field can pull the contacts together and close a relay that was never commanded on.
claims.quote_verbatim: you sometimes need to shield that because stray magnetic fields can then actually make those pieces of metal come together
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Reed relays are the preferred choice for switching low-level signals, where contact quality and low leakage matter more than current-carrying capacity.
claims.quote_verbatim: reed relays, if you don't know, are the duck's guts for low signal level stuff
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Arcing at relay contacts pits the metal and alters the surface material, so a worn relay can develop non-linear, rectifying behaviour instead of acting as a clean switch.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you get arcing or anything like that, you start to pit there and you change the whole material, basically. Your relay can turn into a freaking diode.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Relay contacts wear mechanically from repeated impact, and any air inside the package allows the contact surfaces to oxidise over time.
claims.quote_verbatim: But if you smack two pieces of metal together enough times, you're going to start wearing on it. Exactly. If there's any air in there, you can create oxidation

claims.claim_text: A domestic PIR alarm sensor uses a relay rated for ten million operations, because the contact cycles every time motion is detected, around the clock for years.
claims.quote_verbatim: they've got a very high reliability relay rated for 10 million changes
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Distributor parametric search will not surface a part from qualitative requirements like small and cheap; finding the right relay meant guessing the one technology keyword the vendor indexes it under.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're on a site and you're looking for a relay. You know that, right? But you can't necessarily type in low cost and small and get all the things you need.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: MEMS relays exist as very small single-pole double-throw parts in LGA packages, offering mechanical contact behaviour at chip scale.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was a MEMS relay. Ah, yes. A microelectrical mechanical system, right? That's what MEMS stands for. And so, we found one. And it is. It is very tiny. It's an LGA package, right?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Digital isolator chips provide an alternative to relays for galvanic isolation by placing two dies in one package with a pair of coils between them, forming an on-package transformer.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have two chips in there. And then, in between, they put two coils. And basically, it's a transformer.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The same in-package coil technique now supports isolated DC-to-DC conversion, not just isolated data links such as USB.
claims.quote_verbatim: And they're actually doing even low power switchers now. Like, they're DC to DC power switchers, right? And basically, it's just two chips in there with these coils.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A good low-power reed relay needs only about five milliamps of coil drive current, which sets the benchmark any miniature relay alternative has to beat.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because a good low power read relay will take like five milliamps or something like that
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: An experienced practitioner argues there is a core list of devices an electrical engineer must understand — the relay, the BJT, the SCR — and that formal courses skip the connection between them, such as treating an SCR as a solid-state relay.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got to know what a relay is. You've got to know what a BJT is. You've got to know what a SCR is. Think about it. Nobody teaches SCR as a relay.
claims.speaker: Larry Sears
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Larry Sears - Hexagram Hardware Holism

claims.claim_text: The practical way to identify unknown switch or relay terminals is to ring them out with an ohmmeter rather than relying on knowing the pole-and-throw nomenclature.
claims.quote_verbatim: And they don't know what terminals to hook up where. And I tell them well just figure it out for yourself with an ohmmeter.
claims.speaker: Eric Wasatonic
claims.episode_title: FPGA, Xess, 32 Bit - Quirky Qualitative Questions

claims.claim_text: A university lab supervisor observes that students routinely cannot operate a relay because they do not realise it contains a separately driven coil distinct from the switched contacts.
claims.quote_verbatim: Students don't even know how to operate relays. They have no idea that there's a coil in there.
claims.speaker: Eric Wasatonic
claims.episode_title: FPGA, Xess, 32 Bit - Quirky Qualitative Questions

claims.claim_text: The switching hardware in common use spans several distinct families with different terminal arrangements: miniature reed relays, solid-state relays, and conventional electromechanical relays in a range of sizes.
claims.quote_verbatim: And then of course there's very tiny reed relays here, solid state relay, and just standard relays, big and small.
claims.speaker: Eric Wasatonic
claims.episode_title: FPGA, Xess, 32 Bit - Quirky Qualitative Questions

claims.claim_text: Switching the output of a rotary phase converter into a step-up transformer required a relay rated at 14 kVA.
claims.quote_verbatim: a box with a 14 KVA relay in it
claims.speaker: Shaun Meehan
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Shaun Meehan - Doctiloquent Dove Deployer

claims.claim_text: The relay was deliberately oversized: the calculated requirement was roughly four to four and a half kVA, and margin was added on top so the contact would reliably handle the load.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think it worked out to be like at least four, four and a half KVA with like some margin that I want to make sure that like this trend, this relay would handle
claims.speaker: Shaun Meehan
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Shaun Meehan - Doctiloquent Dove Deployer

claims.claim_text: Start-up sequencing matters with rotary phase converters: the transformer must be switched in only after the converter is already spinning, otherwise energising it can destroy the converter.
claims.quote_verbatim: Cause I had to turn on the transformer with the, uh, after the rotary phase converter was started.
claims.speaker: Shaun Meehan
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Shaun Meehan - Doctiloquent Dove Deployer

claims.claim_text: A safety interlock on delivery trucks uses a relay driven by one controller to signal a second controller that it is safe to release the handbrake, preventing rollaway while the engine idles to run the delivery pump.
claims.quote_verbatim: his board drives a relay and the relay drives the signal, which tells the my controller, a second my controller to let go of the handbrakes for the truck and make it safe
claims.speaker: Ronald Sousa
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ronald Sousa of Hash Define Electronics

claims.claim_text: A Wi-Fi connected garden controller switched AC outlets for pumps and lights through Omron relays, driven by temperature, humidity, light and soil-conductivity readings.
claims.quote_verbatim: connected to Omron relays to control AC outlets hooked up to a pump or a light
claims.speaker: Luke Iseman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: For current-measurement range switching there are three options — relays, N-channel MOSFETs, or a mix — and relays, while clean, are far too slow for fast automatic ranging.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can do it with relays, which is super slow. Or you can do it with N-channel MOSFETs or a combination of all three, and it gets super messy in every single case.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Integrated parts with current shunt in the name are designed for power monitoring, not for low-current measurement, so they are a poor starting point for a microamp-capable instrument.
claims.quote_verbatim: anything with current shunt in the name basically is not meant for low current stuff, basically. It's meant for power monitoring
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A relay can serve as a hard power kill for a networked appliance, physically cutting mains to a smart speaker so it cannot listen regardless of its firmware state.
claims.quote_verbatim: there was some secondary control mechanism that basically just cut a relay to the power for the Amazon Echo so that you couldn't listen anymore
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Electromechanical pinball machines implemented scorekeeping, carry, reset and target logic entirely from relays, stepper units and solenoids, with no processor of any kind.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm talking all you have is relays and steppers and solenoids and that's it.
claims.speaker: John Day

claims.claim_text: Debugging relay logic is a schematic-tracing exercise rather than a software one: the technician follows the circuit through each relay contact in turn, probing with clip leads and indicators to localise the fault.
claims.quote_verbatim: So it's not code. It's a schematic. So you stare it down and you're like following, you know, you're tracing everything through each relay contact to try to identify where the problem may occur.
claims.speaker: John Day

claims.claim_text: Switching 5,000 amps required a purpose-built pneumatic contactor rather than any conventional relay.
claims.quote_verbatim: Something that could switch the 5,000 amps. And that was like this big new pneumatic contactor.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: At extreme current the contact mechanism scales up to a pneumatic ram forcing one large metal plate against another; the plates are the relay contact.
claims.quote_verbatim: This big ram just jammed this big metal plate against another metal plate. And it was like that's the relay contact.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Breadboard prototyping remains acceptable provided the builder respects its limits, and slow loads such as relay circuits fall comfortably inside those limits.
claims.quote_verbatim: As long as people know the, uh, the restrictions, you know, like relays, slow stuff, no big deal.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Relay coils are inductive loads and need a freewheeling, or flyback, diode across the coil to clamp the kickback transient generated when drive current is removed.
claims.quote_verbatim: Are you doing like kickbacks and stuff like that for a relay? Yes. Yes. Fly back. Yeah. Free wheeling diodes on a relay.

claims.claim_text: Inductive kickback transients from a switching circuit are a credible cause of downstream damage: a Raspberry Pi CM4 already running near its voltage limit failed, with spikes from the upstream switching circuit the suspected trigger.
claims.quote_verbatim: I was already pretty close to the voltage limit on the CM4. And then I think a little bit of a spiky spikies. Uh, I think I probably put it over the edge.

claims.claim_text: An open-drain output can sink current into relay coils and solenoids, but it cannot drive an H-bridge, which needs both high-side and low-side drive.
claims.quote_verbatim: No, because it's an open drain. You wouldn't be driving a H-bridge with it, but you'd be driving relays. You'd be driving solenoids.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Mechanical relays remain attractive in precision analog signal paths because they have effectively zero leakage and very few parasitics, their main penalty being some added capacitance.
claims.quote_verbatim: They have zero leakage for all practical purposes. And, uh, they have very few parasitics. They have some extra capacitance
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty
claims.episode_title: The Joulescope Upgrade with Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: The audible clicking of a bench multimeter changing ranges is relay actuation, and it is a direct indicator of how slow relay-based range switching is compared with FET switching.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's also like FETs in the, in the path as well, but like when you hear clicks, it's not that fast
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Joulescope Upgrade with Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: Replacing relay range switching with MOSFETs allows the range decision to be made in under a microsecond using dedicated comparators and a separate analog channel feeding an FPGA.
claims.quote_verbatim: we make the decision in under a microsecond, which is, you know, we have dedicated hardware to do that comparators and a separate analog channel
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty
claims.episode_title: The Joulescope Upgrade with Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: Solid-state range switches must be driven fast but with a controlled edge, because uncontrolled MOSFET gate drive injects charge into the measured signal; propagation through the analog path still costs a few microseconds.
claims.quote_verbatim: We have a super fast, but controlled drive to the MOSFETs to, to mitigate charge injection problems.
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty
claims.episode_title: The Joulescope Upgrade with Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: Industrial carrier boards offer relay modules as a standard option so a compute module can drive conventional 24 volt DC machine interfaces alongside opto-isolated IO and serial links.
claims.quote_verbatim: And also, yeah, customizable relays, for example, default relays to 24 volt DC machines.
claims.speaker: Saber Kaygusuz

claims.claim_text: The programmable logic controller was created to replace plant control panels that had been built from relays, switches and indicator lamps with a single reprogrammable box.
claims.quote_verbatim: they were making controls and they were doing it using relays and switches and indicator lamps. But he thought it would be more advantageous if there was a box
claims.speaker: Don Wilcher
claims.episode_title: Engineering Education with Dr Don Wilcher

claims.claim_text: Ladder logic was chosen as the PLC programming model specifically so that plant electricians and technicians could apply their existing relay-logic knowledge without learning a new discipline.
claims.quote_verbatim: just basically use the knowledge that the plant floor technician, electrician had meaning like relay ladder logic
claims.speaker: Don Wilcher
claims.episode_title: Engineering Education with Dr Don Wilcher

claims.claim_text: Layering an automation system means keeping the firmware that actually closes the relay trivially simple and stable, and pushing changeable scheduling and priority logic up to a higher-level interface.
claims.quote_verbatim: you should basically have some firmware that like just says, listen for signal, flip the relay. Right. You want it to have like, that's dead simple. It always works.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Automotive ABS pump drive moved from a relay in older designs to a totem-pole MOSFET pair in newer ones.
claims.quote_verbatim: the older style used a relay to actually drive the pump motor thing. Whereas, I believe mine uses a pair of MOSFETs, like a totem pole pair of MOSFETs.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A permanently running ABS pump points to a shorted switching element — a shorted motor, a shorted drive transistor pair, or welded relay contacts depending on which drive topology the unit uses.
claims.quote_verbatim: most people thought that it was either a shorted out motor in it, or it was a shorted out drive transistor pair in it. Or it was a shorted out relay, depending on which one it used
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Off-the-shelf home automation relay boards are commonly specified around four channels rated for 240 volts at 20 amps, adequate for mains-level switching.
claims.quote_verbatim: Just like four, four relays that can do 120 volts and 20 amps. Okay. Sorry. 240, 240 at 20 amps.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Grid-tied solar inverters curtail output by simply opening relay contacts inside the box to disconnect from the grid, rather than by any sophisticated regulation.
claims.quote_verbatim: well, they're just opening up the, the switches. Right. Turning off the relay.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

attribution_notes: ep=93 passage is flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE with speaker=Chris Gammell, but the content ('my company would love to do that. We do that') is the guest describing his own employer's solid-state switching products, so both claims are attributed to Tom LeMense.

ep=220 passage is flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE with speaker=Dave Jones, but the words describe the speaker's own shop build-out (rotary phase converter, traded three 1 kVA relays for a 14 kVA unit), which is the guest's story; attributed to Shaun Meehan.
ep=485 passage is flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE with speaker=John Day; content is the guest describing his own electromechanical pinball restoration hobby, so John Day is correct anyway.

ep=607 passages [30] and [31] overlap and carry conflicting speaker labels (Dave Jones and Chris Gammell) despite containing the same text. The Joulescope internals (sub-microsecond range decision, controlled MOSFET drive, FPGA) are the guest's own product, attributed to Matt Liberty. The 'old multimeter clicking through ranges' aside is a host observation and is attributed to Chris Gammell.

ep=88 passage is labelled speaker=Chris Gammell, but the Mida reed-switch factory video is elsewhere (ep=94) identified as Dave Jones's favourite; the Mida manufacturer claim is attributed to Dave Jones and the plain reed-switch definition left null because the two voices alternate mid-passage.

ep=94 passage [11] is labelled Dave Jones, but the passage ends 'or like Dave's child will be doing in a few months', so the alarm-sensor / 10-million-operation anecdote is Chris Gammell; the preceding contact-wear line is left null because the turn boundary is unclear.

ep=94 passage [9] is labelled Chris Gammell, but the closing reed-relay recommendation is answered by Dave ('Dave, you love that video, right? Oh, yeah. See, reed relays...'), so that claim is attributed to Dave Jones.
ep=94 passage [13] is labelled Chris Gammell; the closing drive-current question and the five-milliamp figure come from the other voice, which is Dave Jones.
ep=293 passage is labelled Dave Jones, but the speaker refers to Dave in the third person ('build it like Dave did', 'Like Dave's saying'), so those claims are attributed to Chris Gammell.
ep=551 passage [27]: the flyback/freewheeling-diode exchange and the damaged CM4 anecdote alternate between the two hosts with no clear boundary, so speaker is left null.

ep=608 and ep=620 passages are labelled with host names but the substantive answers are the guests describing their own product line and their own field, so they are attributed to Saber Kaygusuz and Don Wilcher respectively.

ep=75 passage mixes the interviewer's restatement with the guest's answer; the air-coil description is the guest's (Ben Krasnow) and the restatement of the mechanism is the interviewer's (Chris Gammell).
